_why: Measured 2026-09-03 over 29 dual-surface design audits: twice `exec agy` ran the full 30-minute timeout AFTER agy finished — result event written, `.done` marker present within ~4 min — because the wrapper waited on the pid. The caller paid the whole wait and got rc=124, which a coordinator reads as 'no verdict' and re-dispatches work already on disk. Each row restores one way the wait goes back to the pid, or one way the new signal fires when it must not.

mutations.name: the-result-event-no-longer-ends-the-wait
mutations._mechanism: THE defect restored: the wrapper waits on the pid again and a finished agy costs the full timeout plus a misleading rc=124.

mutations.name: any-event-counts-as-completion
mutations._mechanism: `init` and `step_update` are mid-turn. Matching any event ends EVERY wait on the first line the agent writes, killing live agents and returning rc=0 with no response — strictly worse than the linger it replaces.

mutations.name: a-named-log-reads-as-completion-regardless-of-content
mutations._mechanism: Fail-open on the signal itself: naming a log is treated as the turn being done, so every wait ends on the first poll — including for a log that does not exist. 'I could not look' spelled the same way as 'the turn is done', the shape this repo keeps paying for. Aimed HERE and not at the `-s` test: `-s` is an optimisation, and a row against it SURVIVED because a missing or empty log is already refused by grep finding nothing. The property lives in grep's exit status.
mutations.find:
if [ -n "$log" ] && [ -s "$log" ]; then
    # Only the TERMINAL event. `init`/`step_update` are mid-turn, and matching any
    # event would end every wait on the first line the agent wrote. Tail-bounded
    # because this runs on a poll and the transcript can be megabytes.
    # Scoped to THIS run's lines, exactly as `_agy_ndjson_response` is. The log is
    # APPENDED to across passes, so an unscoped grep sees the PREVIOUS pass's `result`
    # and kills the new child on its first poll — measured: `test_verb_passes_one`
    # dropped to `dispatch_count == 0`, a defect strictly worse than the linger.
    tail -n "+$(( after + 1 ))" "$log" 2>/dev/null | tail -c 65536 \
      | grep -aqE '"event"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*"result"' && return 0
  fi

mutations.name: a-completed-run-still-reports-the-timeout-convention
mutations._mechanism: rc=124 on a run that DID finish is exactly what makes a coordinator re-dispatch work already on disk — the misleading half of the original defect, kept after the wait itself was fixed.

mutations.name: the-timeout-ceiling-is-lost
mutations._mechanism: With the deadline branch gone a no-signal hang waits forever, which is worse than the 124 it replaced: the linger at least ended.

mutations.name: the-done-marker-is-ignored
mutations._mechanism: The report-file transport's own completion signal is dropped, so a run whose report is on disk keeps waiting on the pid.

mutations.name: the-completion-check-is-not-scoped-to-this-run
mutations._mechanism: The log is APPENDED to across passes, so an unscoped grep sees the PREVIOUS pass's `result` event and kills the new child on its first poll. Caught by the existing suite when this shipped unscoped: `test_verb_passes_one` fell to `dispatch_count == 0`. A dispatcher that never dispatches is strictly worse than the linger it replaces.
